facts.statehood_note: Hawaiʻi became the 50th and newest state. Statehood Day is an official state holiday. Before statehood it was a U.S. territory (Organic Act signed April 30, 1900).
facts.motto: Ua Mau ke Ea o ka ʻĀina i ka Pono ("The life of the land is perpetuated in righteousness")
borders: Pacific Ocean (Hawaiʻi is an island chain and borders no other state)

symbols.name: "Hawaiʻi Ponoʻī," words by King Kalākaua (1874), music by Henry Berger

facts.name_origin: No one is certain. One Hawaiian tradition says the islands are named for Hawaiʻiloa, a great fisherman and navigator who settled the Big Island; the name is also related to other Polynesian homeland names such as Havaiʻi and Savaiʻi. Captain Cook called them the Sandwich Islands in 1778, but the name Hawaiʻi replaced that by the 1840s.

government.chambers: Hawaiʻi State Senate (25 senators, 4-year terms) and Hawaiʻi House of Representatives (51 representatives, 2-year terms); 76 lawmakers in all
government.executive: Governor (4-year term, no more than 2 full terms in a row), with a lieutenant governor; the governor signs or vetoes bills and leads the executive departments
government.courts: Hawaiʻi Supreme Court (a chief justice and 4 associate justices, 5 total; 10-year terms, chosen by the governor from a Judicial Selection Commission list and confirmed by the state senate), plus the Intermediate Court of Appeals, circuit courts, and district courts. The court meets in Aliʻiōlani Hale.
government.local: 4 main counties (City and County of Honolulu, Hawaiʻi County, Maui County, and Kauaʻi County); tiny Kalawao County (the Kalaupapa settlement on Molokaʻi) is counted with Maui County in state population figures. Hawaiʻi has no separate city or town governments below the counties.
government.constitution: Adopted by voters on November 7, 1950, nine years before statehood, and in effect since August 21, 1959; it is Hawaiʻi's first and only state constitution and has been amended many times since. The 1978 Constitutional Convention created the Office of Hawaiian Affairs.
government.kid_line: "English and Hawaiian shall be the official languages of Hawaii" (Hawaiʻi State Constitution, Article XV, Section 4). Article XV, Section 5 makes "Ua mau ke ea o ka aina i ka pono" the state motto.

long_ago.nation: Kānaka Maoli (Native Hawaiians): the first voyagers
long_ago.about: Polynesian voyagers from the Marquesas Islands area were the first people to settle Hawaiʻi, about 1000 to 1200 AD. They crossed more than 2,000 miles of ocean in double-hulled canoes, steering by the stars, winds, currents, and seabirds, and brought pigs, dogs, chickens, taro, sweet potato, coconut, banana, and sugarcane.

long_ago.nation: Kānaka Maoli: life in the ahupuaʻa
long_ago.about: Rulers divided the larger islands into districts called moku, and each moku into ahupuaʻa, land sections running from the mountain top to the reef so families had nearly everything they needed. People fished, farmed taro and pounded it into poi, made kapa cloth from bark, and used kapu (rules) to protect fishing and planting.

long_ago.nation: Kānaka Maoli: chant, song, and hula
long_ago.about: Native Hawaiians kept their history alive through oli (chant), mele (song), and hula (dance), and honored akua (gods) and ʻaumakua (family guardian spirits). In Hawaiian tradition, Kīlauea volcano is the home of Pele, the volcano deity.
Kamehameha I united the islands into one kingdom in 1810. The kingdom was an independent nation: the United States signed treaties with Hawaiian monarchs in 1826, 1842, 1849, 1875, and 1887.

long_ago.nation: The Hawaiian Kingdom under Queen Liliʻuokalani
long_ago.about: Liliʻuokalani became queen in 1891. In 1893 she was overthrown by a small group of mostly American businessmen backed by U.S. naval forces, and she and her people protested peacefully for years afterward.

today.about: The Native Hawaiian community lives throughout the islands today; the U.S. Department of the Interior works with it through its Office of Native Hawaiian Relations, the state's Office of Hawaiian Affairs (created 1978, led by elected Hawaiian trustees) works to better conditions for Native Hawaiians, and the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands manages about 200,000 acres of homestead land set aside by the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act of 1920.

first_peoples.today_note: Native Hawaiians are not organized as a federally recognized tribe, and there is no federally recognized Native Hawaiian government today. In 1993 the U.S. Congress passed Public Law 103-150, formally apologizing to Native Hawaiians for the U.S. role in the 1893 overthrow; it also says it does not settle any claims.
sites: ʻIolani Palace, Honolulu: built by King Kalākaua and later home of Queen Liliʻuokalani; the only royal palace on U.S. soil, and the place where she was imprisoned in 1895
Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park (Hawaiʻi Island): Kīlauea, the home of Pele in Hawaiian tradition
Haleakalā National Park (Maui): Pōhaku Pālaha, where Maui's moku (land districts) meet, considered by some Native Hawaiians the piko (sacred center) of Maui
Papahānaumokuākea (Northwestern Hawaiian Islands): the first mixed natural and cultural World Heritage site in the United States (2010)

history.event: Polynesian voyagers from the Marquesas Islands area settle the Hawaiian Islands, sailing double-hulled canoes more than 2,000 miles by stars, winds, and birds.
British Captain James Cook reaches the islands and calls them the Sandwich Islands. His arrival brings outside contact that changes Hawaiian life dramatically.
Captain George Vancouver gives cattle to Kamehameha I, the start of ranching in Hawaiʻi.
Kamehameha I (Kamehameha the Great) unites the eight major islands into one Hawaiian Kingdom; he rules until his death in 1819.
More than 100 American Protestant missionaries come to Hawaiʻi. In 1823 Betsey Stockton, a Black teacher born into slavery, opens Maui's first school for common people at Lahaina.
The United States recognizes the Hawaiian Kingdom as an independent nation and signs the first of several treaties with it (more follow in 1842, 1849, 1875, and 1887).
Kamehameha III brings vaqueros (cowboys) from Mexico and Spain to teach Hawaiians to herd cattle; Hawaiian cowboys become known as paniolo.

Kamehameha III, under pressure from foreigners, begins the Great Māhele, replacing the ahupuaʻa system with private land titles. Many Native Hawaiians never filed claims, and over time much land passed to foreign owners.
The Kuleana Act lets commoners claim small family plots, and the Masters and Servants Act sets up a contract labor system that brings plantation workers from overseas.
During the U.S. Civil War, sugar from Louisiana stops, and Hawaiʻi's sugar plantations grow quickly.

A reciprocity treaty with the United States lets Hawaiian sugar enter the U.S. tax-free, making planters rich and tying Hawaiʻi's economy to the U.S. Plantations later recruit workers from China, Japan, the Philippines, Korea, Portugal, Spain, and Puerto Rico.

With U.S. Minister John L. Stevens' help and U.S. naval forces landed near ʻIolani Palace, a 'Committee of Safety' of American and European sugar planters, missionary descendants, and businessmen overthrows Queen Liliʻuokalani. She yields 'to the superior force of the United States of America' under protest to avoid bloodshed.

President Grover Cleveland calls the overthrow an 'act of war' and asks for the queen's return, but the new government refuses and declares the Republic of Hawaii (July 4, 1894). Liliʻuokalani is forced to give up the throne in 1895 while imprisoned in ʻIolani Palace. Native Hawaiians protest annexation with petitions and delegations to Washington.

The U.S. annexes Hawaiʻi on July 7, 1898 (Newlands Resolution), taking about 1.8 million acres of crown and government lands without the consent of Native Hawaiians. Hawaiʻi becomes a territory in 1900 and the 50th state on August 21, 1959.

trailblazers.name: Queen Liliʻuokalani
trailblazers.group: Native Hawaiian woman, last monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom
trailblazers.text: She became queen in 1891 and tried to give her people a new constitution in 1893, but was overthrown that year and later imprisoned. She led years of 'resolute and peaceful resistance' to annexation, and she was also a gifted composer who wrote 'Aloha ʻOe' in 1878.

trailblazers.name: Anthony D. Allen (Alani)
trailblazers.text: Born into slavery in New York, he escaped at about 24, later bought his freedom, and settled in Hawaiʻi, where he served Kamehameha the Great and received land in Waikīkī. He built a school, the first carriage road up Mānoa Valley, and ran Honolulu's first hospital for American sailors.

trailblazers.name: Betsey Stockton
trailblazers.text: Born into slavery in Princeton, New Jersey, she gained her freedom and came to Hawaiʻi in 1823. Assigned to Lahaina, Maui, she learned Hawaiian and started Maui's first school for common people, on the site of today's Lahainaluna School.

trailblazers.name: Duke Kahanamoku
trailblazers.text: He won Olympic gold in the 100-meter freestyle swim in 1912 and again in 1920, and he shared Hawaiian surfing with the world, bringing it to the U.S. Atlantic coast in 1914. He served as Honolulu's sheriff for decades and was named Hawaiʻi's Ambassador of Aloha in 1960.

trailblazers.name: Daniel K. Inouye
trailblazers.group: Japanese American man, soldier and U.S. senator
trailblazers.text: Born in Honolulu, he fought in World War II with the 442nd Regimental Combat Team of Japanese American soldiers and lost his right arm in combat, later receiving the Medal of Honor. He was one of Hawaiʻi's first members of Congress after statehood and won election to the U.S. Senate in 1962.

trailblazers.name: Patsy Takemoto Mink
trailblazers.text: Born in Pāʻia, Maui, she won a seat in the U.S. House in 1964, becoming the first woman of color and first Asian American woman in Congress. She was a main author of Title IX (1972), which bans sex discrimination in schools that get federal money, and is called 'the Mother of Title IX.'

landforms: Eight main islands and 124 islets, all made by volcanoes
Mauna Loa, the largest active volcano on Earth
Mauna Kea, the world's tallest volcano measured from the ocean floor
Kīlauea, one of the most active volcanoes on Earth
Haleakalā ("House of the Sun"), the giant volcano of Maui
waters: Coral reefs around the islands and in Papahānaumokuākea
Honolua Bay (Maui), where Hōkūleʻa set sail in 1976
geography.regions: Hawaiʻi is a chain of more than 80 volcanoes stretching thousands of miles: the eight main islands in the southeast (Kauaʻi is the oldest, about 5 million years old, and Hawaiʻi Island is the youngest), and the low islands and atolls of the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands.

ecosystems.name: Coral reefs
ecosystems.about: Papahānaumokuākea alone protects about 3.5 million acres of coral reef, roughly 70% of all U.S. coral reefs, and about 25% of its species live nowhere else on Earth. Endangered Hawaiian monk seals breed there and threatened green sea turtles nest there.

ecosystems.name: Native rain forests
ecosystems.about: Native honeycreepers such as the ʻapapane and ʻiʻiwi feed on the red blossoms of ʻōhiʻa lehua trees. Some forest birds, like the kiwikiu (Maui parrotbill), are critically endangered, with very few left, and introduced avian malaria is a threat to native birds.

ecosystems.name: Seabird islands
ecosystems.about: The Northwestern Hawaiian Islands are home to more than 14 million seabirds of 22 species, including the world's largest colonies of Laysan and black-footed albatross.

science.weather: Warm all year, but Hawaiʻi faces hurricanes (Hurricane ʻIniki hit Kauaʻi and Oʻahu on September 11, 1992, and Hurricane ʻIwa in 1982), tsunamis (the April 1, 1946 tsunami killed 159 people, and the May 22, 1960 tsunami from Chile killed 61, mostly at Hilo), earthquakes, and volcanic eruptions.
science.resources: Tourism (the visitor industry) is Hawaiʻi's largest source of income, and defense (military spending) is another top industry; sugar and pineapple were long the main farm exports. Cattle ranching has been part of island life since 1793.
science.highlight: The Hawaiian hot spot: a fixed plume of hot material deep in the Earth melts rock into magma, while the Pacific Plate slides northwest about 2 to 4 inches a year like a conveyor belt. That built a chain of more than 80 volcanoes, and Mauna Loa rises more than 30,000 feet from the sea floor.

g3_ss.title: Hawaiʻi's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find the islands and the four counties on a map, learn what the governor, the 76 lawmakers, and the 5 Supreme Court justices do, and read the constitution line that makes English and Hawaiian the official languages.

g3_ss.title: Hawaiʻi's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Follow the Polynesian voyagers across the Pacific, build a paper ahupuaʻa from mountain to reef, and learn how taro, poi, kapa, chant, and hula kept families and stories alive.

g3_ss.title: Hawaiʻi Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Meet Queen Liliʻuokalani, Betsey Stockton, Duke Kahanamoku, and Patsy Mink, then make a trading card for each that tells one brave thing they did.

g45_ss.title: Kānaka Maoli: Voyagers and the Ahupuaʻa
g45_ss.plan: Study wayfinding by stars, winds, and birds (and Hōkūleʻa's 1976 voyage to Tahiti), then compare the ahupuaʻa land system with how land is divided today.

g45_ss.title: The Hawaiian Kingdom, 1810 to 1876
g45_ss.plan: Trace Kamehameha I's united kingdom, U.S. treaties with an independent Hawaiʻi, the missionaries, the paniolo, and the 1848 Māhele, asking who gained and who lost land.

g45_ss.title: Sugar, the Overthrow, and Statehood
g45_ss.plan: Use the reciprocity treaty, plantation labor from Asia and Europe, Liliʻuokalani's 1893 protest statement, and the 1993 Apology Resolution to explain how Hawaiʻi went from kingdom to territory to the 50th state.

g3_sci.title: Islands Made by Volcanoes
g3_sci.plan: Model how lava builds an island, meet Kīlauea and Mauna Loa, and learn why Kauaʻi is old and Hawaiʻi Island is young.

g3_sci.title: Life on the Reef
g3_sci.plan: Explore coral reefs with the humuhumunukunukuapuaʻa, green sea turtles, and Hawaiian monk seals, and list ways people protect the reef.

g3_sci.title: Birds Found Nowhere Else
g3_sci.plan: Meet the nēnē, ʻapapane, and ʻiʻiwi, match bird beaks to ʻōhiʻa lehua flowers, and learn why some island birds are endangered.

g45_sci.title: The Hawaiian Hot Spot
g45_sci.plan: Use a conveyor-belt model of the Pacific Plate moving 2 to 4 inches a year over a fixed hot spot to explain the 80-volcano chain, and order the islands by age.

g45_sci.title: Hurricanes and Tsunamis
g45_sci.plan: Compare how hurricanes (ʻIniki, 1992) and tsunamis (1946 and 1960 at Hilo) form, map the damage, and write a family safety plan.

g45_sci.title: Papahānaumokuākea: Protecting an Ocean
g45_sci.plan: Investigate the largest fully protected conservation area in the U.S., its 14 million seabirds and endemic reef species, and why it is both a natural and cultural treasure.
